incidents.name: VerifierExit exit-proof verification always returning true
incidents.notes: ZKSwap 1.0's VerifierExit began verifyExitProof() with an unconditional `return true`, so once the rollup was pushed into Exodus Mode the attacker's forged exit proofs against the frozen state root were accepted and the L1 bridge released its balances.

sources.ref: callTracer review of the fake-exit tx: the attacker contract 0x2D3103c8Fdd9d9411E24f555fdad6B22F29F613A calls the ZKSwap bridge proxy 0x8ECa806Aecc86CE90Da803b080Ca4E3A9b8097ad (selector 0xd6973fc6) which STATICCALLs the VerifierExit proxy 0x961369d3...f521f 15 times with selector 0xc81a27ad, every one returning 0x...01 for a forged proof; bridge storage slot 6 holds the VerifierExit address, both proxies were created in the same 2021-02-12 deployment tx by 0x7d1a14eed7af8e26f24bf08ba6ed7a339abcf037 (not the attacker), and the VerifierExit proxy has emitted no logs at all in its lifetime, so it was never upgraded; the exodus trigger was tx 0xfdb93e00f3b1d24303db7f43eaa5ef50d3fde957ddeec7c0feb8c5497ba11182

deployment-basis recheck (storage, not events): the VerifierExit proxy's single DELEGATECALL in the exploit tx (selector 0xc81a27ad) goes to 0xd12f4d8329584f36aed67f807f42d9a02beb9534, and the EIP-1967 implementation slot holds that address at the creation block 11841962, at the incident block 22882195 and at all 41 evenly spaced samples in between; the proxy runtime is byte-identical at both blocks. The always-true verifier really was the 2021 deployment; 1607.6 days.
